---
title: "Figure 4: LA5: Drivers of Change in Growth, 2026"
---

![Python: `python/fig-4-0.py`](../images/python/fig-4-0.png)

A waterfall chart. It decomposes the change in LA5 growth between 2025 and
2026 into contributions from terms of trade, financial conditions,
uncertainty and a residual. Each contribution is a bar that starts where the
previous one ended: positive contributions step up, negative ones step down.
Together they add up to the total change in growth, shown as the last bar,
which stands on zero.

A waterfall is a good way to show a decomposition when the parts have
different signs. A stacked bar would hide that some parts offset others.

**New in this chart:**

- floating bars;
- a colour per bar;
- labels with line breaks under the bars.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 5 rows:

| category | Lower band | Upper band |
|---|---|---|
| Terms of trade | 0.000 | 0.187 |
| Financial conditions | 0.187 | 0.443 |
| Uncertainty | 0.328 | 0.302 |
| Residual | 0.079 | 0.249 |
| Change in growth, 2026 vs. 2025 | 0.000 | 0.079 |

Excel has no waterfall chart type in older versions. The usual workaround is
a stacked column chart:

- **An invisible series** (`Lower band`) lifts each bar to the bottom of
  where it should float.
- **A visible series** (`Upper band`) is the height of the bar itself.

The bars are:

- **Terms of trade**: from 0 to 0.187.
- **Financial conditions**: from 0.187 up to 0.630.
- **Uncertainty**: a negative contribution, so its bar runs *down* from 0.630
  to 0.328. It is drawn as a bar from 0.328 with height 0.302.
- **Residual**: from 0.079 to 0.328.
- **The total change**: from 0 to 0.079.

## The script

```python
bar_colours = {
    "Terms of trade": "#78C51C",
    "Financial conditions": "#78C51C",
    "Uncertainty": "#E1251B",
    "Residual": "#B6B7B8",
    "Change in growth, 2026 vs. 2025": "#5B2A73",
}
labels = {
    "Terms of trade": "Terms of\ntrade",
    ...
    "Change in growth, 2026 vs. 2025": "Change in\ngrowth, 2026\nvs. 2025",
}
```

Two dictionaries, both keyed by the category name:

- **`bar_colours`** gives each bar its colour. Positive contributions are
  green, the negative one is red, the residual grey and the total purple.
- **`labels`** gives the text under each bar, with line breaks where the
  published chart has them.

```python
x = np.arange(len(data))
ax.bar(x, data["Upper band"], bottom=data["Lower band"], width=1.0,
       color=[bar_colours[c] for c in data["category"]])
```

One call draws the whole waterfall. `bottom=` lifts each bar by its `Lower
band`, which is exactly what the invisible Excel series did. There is no need
to draw the invisible series at all.

- **Bar width.** `width=1.0` makes the bars touch, as in the published chart.
- **Colours.** `color=[...]` gives one colour per bar.

```python
ax.set_xticks(x, [labels[c] for c in data["category"]])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=3, pad=5, labelsize=9)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 0.8, 0.2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")
```

The labels are looked up in the `labels` dictionary in the order of the
data. `[labels[c] for c in data["category"]]` is a list comprehension: for
each category name `c`, in the order of the rows, it takes the label with
line breaks. The same pattern picks the colours above. Looking up by name,
rather than relying on the order of the dictionary, means the labels and
colours stay with the right bars even if the rows come in a different order.

- **Tick marks.** `length=3` keeps short tick marks under the bars, between
  the labels and the axis, as in the published chart.
- **The x-limits** run half a bar beyond the first and last bars, so with
  `width=1.0` the outer bars touch the edges of the plot.
- **The y-axis** runs from 0 to 0.8 in steps of 0.2. `"{x:.1f}"` writes the
  labels with one decimal: 0.0, 0.2, ..., 0.8. See [Number
  formats](../techniques.qmd#sec-number-formats).

There is no legend: the labels under the bars name each contribution, and
the colours only show whether it is positive or negative.

## Changing the chart

- **From contributions to a waterfall.** If you have the contributions
  themselves (for example 0.187, 0.443, -0.302, -0.249) rather than Excel's
  helper series, compute the floating bars with a running total:

  ```python
  contributions = np.array([0.187, 0.443, -0.302, -0.249])
  ends = np.cumsum(contributions)
  starts = ends - contributions
  bottoms = np.minimum(starts, ends)
  heights = np.abs(contributions)
  ```

  Then add the total as a last bar from 0 to `ends[-1]`.
- **Colours from the sign.** Instead of typing a colour per bar, choose
  green or red automatically (the residual and the total would then need their own colours):
  `["#78C51C" if c > 0 else "#E1251B" for c in contributions]`.
- **Value labels.** Keep what `ax.bar()` returns and call
  `ax.bar_label(bars, labels=[f"{c:+.2f}" for c in contributions])`; the
  `+` in the format shows the sign.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-4-0.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-4-0.py"}
"""Figure 4: LA5: Drivers of Change in Growth, 2026 (waterfall chart)."""
import numpy as np

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-4-0"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

# In Excel the waterfall is a stacked column chart: an invisible "Lower band"
# lifts each visible "Upper band" bar to the right height.
bar_colours = {
    "Terms of trade": "#78C51C",
    "Financial conditions": "#78C51C",
    "Uncertainty": "#E1251B",
    "Residual": "#B6B7B8",
    "Change in growth, 2026 vs. 2025": "#5B2A73",
}
labels = {
    "Terms of trade": "Terms of\ntrade",
    "Financial conditions": "Financial\nconditions",
    "Uncertainty": "Uncertainty",
    "Residual": "Residual",
    "Change in growth, 2026 vs. 2025": "Change in\ngrowth, 2026\nvs. 2025",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LA5: Drivers of Change in Growth, 2026",
    subtitle="(Percent)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Ahir, H, N Bloom, and D Furceri (2022), “World Uncertainty\n"
        "Index”, NBER Working Paper; Haver Analytics; IMF, World Economic\n"
        "Outlook database; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Aggregate is purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted average.\n"
        "Estimates are obtained from a local projection regression of growth on\n"
        "terms of trade, financial conditions, and uncertainty, controlling for US and\n"
        "China growth and inflation, and country- and year- fixed effects. For\n"
        "methodology and variables included in the financial conditions index, refer\n"
        "to the online annex of the October 2018 Global Financial Stability Report.\n"
        "LA5 = Latin America 5 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru)."
    ),
    caption_size=8.2,
    left=0.4,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.55,
)

x = np.arange(len(data))
ax.bar(x, data["Upper band"], bottom=data["Lower band"], width=1.0,
       color=[bar_colours[c] for c in data["category"]])

ax.set_xticks(x, [labels[c] for c in data["category"]])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=3, pad=5, labelsize=9)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 0.8, 0.2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=3)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
